text:
**The Spare Room**

The flat was always on the third floor, and Daniel always had the keys.

That was the first thing he noticed in the dream: the weight of them in his coat pocket, a heavy ring he didn't remember acquiring, which he would sort through on the landing until he found the right one. Inside, the light was late-September light, thin and gold, falling across floorboards someone had sanded and never furnished. A window looked over a city that was not quite London, in which the river ran the wrong way.

And there was the knowledge, arriving the moment he stepped inside, that he had been paying for this place for years. Direct debit. He had simply forgotten. All that time it had been here, waiting, while he lived elsewhere, in smaller rooms.

Sometimes Rachel was there, standing in the kitchen, which had no appliances, holding a mug. "Well," she would say, without surprise, "it's not as if *I* was going to use it." Other times only her things were: a cardigan on the windowsill, the crime novels she read in the bath. Once, a single tennis shoe in the middle of the empty living room, laces still tied.

He would wake at four or five with the guilt of the dream still on him: not the guilt of a man who has dreamed of his ex-wife but the guilt of waste. All that space. All that light, falling on nothing.

---

The dreams started in February. By April he had stopped pretending they were incidental. He would lie beside Isabel in the dark and list the flats he had actually lived in: Kentish Town, Brixton, the house in Stockwell with the garden Rachel had wanted and then stopped going into, the studio in Bethnal Green where he'd spent eighteen months after the divorce eating standing up. None of them faced a river. None of them had been empty.

It was Isabel who brought it up.

"You're doing it again," she said one Sunday morning, not looking up from her book. "Staring at the ceiling like you've been told the results of a test. If it's the prostate, I'd rather know."

"It's not the prostate. It's a dream. A recurring one."

"Ah." She closed the book on her finger. "Go on, then."

So he told her, and she listened with the stillness she brought to her cello students explaining why they hadn't practised. When he got to Rachel he hesitated, and she said, "Daniel. I was married nine years to a man who alphabetised the spice rack while I was in labour. Nothing you say about Rachel is going to frighten me."

"She's in it. Or her things are. A shoe."

"One shoe?"

"One shoe."

"Well, that's very Freudian," she said, and then, seeing his face, "No, it isn't. I don't know what it is." She drank her tea. "I used to have one about the old house in Leeds. I'd dream I'd moved out but forgotten the cat, and I'd go back and Paul would be making a lasagne, perfectly pleasant, and the cat would be nowhere. For years, that one."

"Did it stop?"

"Eventually. You never notice the last one."

"We didn't have a cat," Daniel said.

"I know. I'm saying it's not about the cat."

---

After that the dream became a household fixture, like a lodger they'd agreed not to mention to the landlord. "Third floor?" she'd ask over breakfast, and he'd say, "Third floor," and she'd pass the marmalade. Not gone, but easier.

He told her the part of the Rachel story he usually skipped. Not the affair, Rachel's, brief and almost apologetic, which everyone had treated as the cause. The years before it, in Stockwell, when they had become extremely competent at living together. They had divided the labour of a life like a set of encyclopaedias, A to L, M to Z. He did the boiler and the car. She did the garden and her mother. They were never unkind. They simply stopped going into each other's rooms.

"So that's your flat," Isabel said. They were walking along the canal. "All that room nobody went into."

"Then why is it still happening? We've been divorced six years. I'm happy here."

She took his arm. A swan went by with the air of a creature that had somewhere to be.

"Maybe it isn't about her," she said. "Maybe she's just the last person who saw it."

---

The keys turned up in May, in the most ordinary way.

Isabel's sister was having a garage sale, and Daniel finally opened the box marked *DAN — MISC* that he had carried through three house moves. He sat on the floor of the spare room with it between his knees. A broken Walkman. A birthday card from his father, signed *Dad.*, with the full stop his father always put after his own name, as if it were a sentence.

And at the bottom, three small brass keys on a cork fishing float, the red paint on its tip worn to pink.

He knew what it was before he'd finished picking it up. His thumb found the groove where he'd once tried to carve his initials and given up after the D.

The summer he was sixteen, his father had bought a secondhand canoe from a man in the pub and kept it chained to a post where the Windrush widened above Burford. His father, who believed anything that could sink would, had threaded the padlock keys onto the cork. That summer and the two after, they went out most weekend mornings, early, before his father's knees went and before Daniel left for university and became, briefly and unforgivably, too interesting for his parents.

He remembered it with startling exactness: the cold paddle shaft before the sun got to it, the mist sitting a foot thick on the water. His father in the stern, teaching him the J-stroke. "You're not steering," his father had said. "You're correcting. All the time. Little bits. Otherwise you go round in circles and blame the river."

They had barely spoken on those mornings. A heron would lift off the bank, and his father would point with his paddle, and that was the whole conversation, and it had been enough.

He had never taken Rachel out in a canoe. He'd suggested it once, and she'd laughed and said she would rather die somewhere warm, and he had put the idea back in its box. He had put a great many things back in boxes over those years. It had seemed a reasonable way to keep a house tidy.

Isabel found him there twenty minutes later. "You've gone very quiet. Is that a fishing float?"

He told her. When he'd finished, she sat on the floor beside him, which, given her back, was a significant gesture, and turned the float over in her hand.

"I've never been in a canoe," she said. "Is it still there?"

"God, no. But you can hire them. There's a place near Lechlade."

She handed the keys back, looking at him over her glasses in that way that made him feel he'd said something more significant than he'd intended.

"Well," she said. "You'd better teach me the J-stroke, then."

---

They went in June, absurdly early, because he insisted the early part was the point. The canoe was red, not green, and the paddles were plastic. None of it was the same, and it didn't matter.

Isabel sat in the bow and gripped her paddle like an unfamiliar instrument. They went into the reeds twice. A family of ducks escorted them with an air of open judgement.

"You're overcorrecting," she called back, without turning around. "We're going like a drunk."

She was right. He was fighting each small drift as though it were a crisis. He made himself slow down. Pull, and twist, and let the boat run. Little bits, all the time. There was mist on the river, and the light coming through it was the thin gold light of the dream, falling now on something: the back of Isabel's neck, her grey hair coming loose from its clip, her shoulders learning the rhythm.

A heron lifted off the bank ahead of them, enormous and unhurried, and Isabel raised her paddle to point at it, and he said, "I see it," and that was the whole conversation.

The dream came back once or twice that summer, but differently. Once, in late August, he opened the door and found the flat had been let to someone else: two pairs of shoes in the hall, a radio playing, a smell of toast. He stood on the threshold a moment, then pulled the door closed, quietly, so as not to disturb them, and went back down the stairs.

He couldn't have said which night was the last one. Isabel had been right about that. You only notice, months later, that you have been sleeping through, and that the keys, the real ones, are hanging on a nail by the back door, the cork float turning a little whenever someone comes in.
